title: Alvarez: Adventures of a Physicist
author: Luis W. Alvarez
note: Selected: physicists Richard Garwin, James Trefil and Alan Lightman praise its explanation of scientific work; the publisher reproduces their reviews, and Garwin's review identity is verified in Physics Today. Goodreads 4.22/68 is positive but small. Scientific memoir qualifies under V3 and is not technical training. Radar, experimental invention and particle research dominate; warfare is one application, so T12=0. Work in the United States has worldwide scientific influence, so T11=0. Personal judgments about colleagues require caution, but no serious veto is established.
notes: Firsthand scientific experience is strong evidence for practice, but recollection and personal disputes require independent historical checks.
Connects instrumentation, wartime engineering, laboratories, particle research and geological evidence.
Offers reusable lessons in experiment selection, instrument building and moving methods between fields.
Explains how measurement tools and experimental choices make discoveries possible.

D=8, moderate confidence from specialist review excerpts, contents and reader reports. Radar, bubble chambers, pyramid imaging and impact evidence add different methods; some personal narrative is less useful. No full-text audit.
Experimental reasoning and research practice retain long-term value.
Direct fit to physics, engineering and scientific organization, with more practical value than a general physics primer.
Nobel-winning experimental physicist assessed favorably by other physicists.
A sequence of investigations makes technical work accessible.
Direct prose focused on decisions and discovery.

title: Monkeyluv: And Other Essays on Our Lives as Animals
author: Robert M. Sapolsky
note: Selected: psychologist Mark F. Lenzenweger's American Journal of Psychiatry review strongly praises the gene-environment explanation and writing; Goodreads 4.24/2,131 corroborates reader enthusiasm. Adult explanatory essays, not a technical course or health-advice program. Behavioral biology is central; disease, religion and social disputes are examples, not the main purpose. Broad cultural analogies merit lower confidence than the neurobiology. No high-confidence foundational veto established for the collection as a whole; this assessment does not import judgments about later Sapolsky books.
notes: Scientific examples support gene-environment interaction, but short essays and broad cultural comparisons leave less room for competing explanations.
Connects genes, physiology, behavior and social setting; limited industrial or institutional integration.
Useful resistance to single-cause explanations and to treating biological effects as context-free.
Explains interacting biological influences through concrete cases.

D=7.5, moderate confidence from Lenzenweger, contents and contrasting reader reports. Different physiological mechanisms add learning, while some introductory sections and short treatment limit depth. Brevity alone is not evidence of density.
Core interaction principles endure; empirical examples reflect research available around 2005.
Mechanistic science offers partial fit, but little computing, engineering or production content.
Specialist author with explicit favorable assessment by a research psychologist.
Lively essays make difficult subjects approachable, though they do not form one cumulative argument.
Controlled humorous explanation without technical training requirements.

title: Kindred: Neanderthal Life, Love, Death and Art
author: Rebecca Wragg Sykes
note: Selected: paleoanthropologist David Frayer and archaeologist Ken Hamilton strongly recommend it, while identifying factual details, uncertain reconstructions and awkward external references. Goodreads 4.04/4,072 supports reader praise, with complaints about dense tool descriptions. This is an explanatory synthesis for adults, not specialist training; brief imagined openings do not make the predominantly nonfiction book fiction. Art is one source of archaeological evidence, not art criticism. Resource use and technology are important, but prehistoric life is the central historical period: approximate endpoint 40,000 years ago gives capped H13=-12. No serious foundational veto established from the inspected reviews.
notes: Broad archaeological evidence underlies the synthesis; sparse evidence, conjecture and specific errors identified by Frayer prevent higher attainment.
Connects tools, materials, mobility, food acquisition, social behavior and genetic evidence.
Useful examples of reconstructing behavior from incomplete physical evidence, with limited direct modern strategy.
Explains constraints on survival and production but cannot firmly establish many social causes.
D=8, moderate confidence from Frayer, Hamilton and reader reports. Distinct sites and tool practices add evidence; dense lithic passages can slow the narrative but are not automatically padding.
Physical evidence and the history of interpreting it retain value; particular reconstructions remain revisable.
Technology and resource use partly fit; most content concerns prehistoric populations.
Specialist author with favorable substantive peer reviews.
Thematic organization and vivid openings improve access, though some readers find it academic.
Evocative prose is generally clear; imaginative passages must be distinguished from findings.
